questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
questions.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $3{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{\sqrt{1-3{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8}{\sqrt{1-(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{25\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/25)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/25}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get  

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (6\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{16\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/16)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/16}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{12-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{12\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/12)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/12}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{12})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{12}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{12}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{12}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{12-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{12})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}{\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\sqrt{12}\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{3}}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1/\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\, & ={\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{25\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/25)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/25}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}} & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{20}{3+75{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{20}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{20}{3+75{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{20}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1/5}\frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{20}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $9x^2 = (3x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \,\textrm d u=\textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{4\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{12}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \dfrac{3}{2 + 50x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{3}{2(1 + 25x^2)} = \dfrac 3 2 \int \dfrac{1}{1+25x^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+u^2}\textrm{d}u =\arctan u +C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $25x^2 = (5x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 5\,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2+50{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

Let $u = 5x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
5\,\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5\,\text{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(5x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+{x}^{2}/2)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this integral now resembles the basic integral for the inverse tangent,

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\,\textrm d u = \arctan{u} + C.
$$

We make the substitution $u=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt 2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡u|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$
